title: Anything you can add and scale
question: What do arrows, polynomials and functions have in common?
hook: They look nothing alike, yet one set of rules is enough to cover all of them.
idea: Linear algebra studies what is shared by anything whose elements can be added together and scaled by numbers.

beats.prompt: In 1637 Descartes introduced coordinates in geometry, so lines and planes could be written as linear equations. Two lines are drawn on a page. What does finding the point where they cross turn into?

choices.label: Solving a system of linear equations
Measuring one angle with a protractor
choices.feedback: It tempts because the lines are drawn, but with coordinates the crossing point is found by computation, not measurement.

choices.label: Taking the slope of a single curve
choices.feedback: A slope belongs to one line; the crossing involves two lines at once, which means two equations.

beats.explain: In this geometry lines and planes are represented by linear equations, so computing their intersections amounts to solving systems of linear equations.

beats.prompt: Match each milestone to the person or place behind it.
pairs: Gaussian elimination in an old text
beats.explain: Linear algebra grew over many centuries, from solving equations to naming and multiplying matrices.

beats.prompt: Put these milestones in order, earliest first.
items: Leibniz first considers determinants for solving linear systems
Cramer uses determinants to give explicit solutions
Peano gives the first modern definition of a vector space

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?
steps: Elements of a vector space only need two operations: adding them and scaling them by numbers.
Polynomials can be elements of a vector space, along with functions and matrices.
But vectors have to be arrows, so these polynomials are not really vectors.
So linear algebra can tell us nothing about polynomials.
beats.explain: The elements of a vector space are called vectors whatever they are, and they can be polynomials, functions or matrices. Linear algebra studies what they share.
